newsitem.title: USA: Maine Public might seek waivers to avoid default.
newsitem.headline: Maine Public might seek waivers to avoid default.

text.p: Maine Public Service, which warned it might default on $15 million of bonds due to problems with the Maine Yankee nuclear plant, on Tuesday said it might ask lenders for waivers to avoid this step.

The utility has said it feared that the high costs tied to the closed nuclear plant might cause it during the first quarter to violate interest coverage tests for both the tax-exempt, revenue bonds and up to $10 million credit line, which only has about $900,000 outstanding.
"All we're doing is saying that based on what we know today and our projections, this is a possible situation," said Larry La Plante, company treasurer.

The official said that the company likely would request the waivers before any default, perhaps one month in advance, but noted that Maine Public Service had not yet held specific talks with banks. "It is a process that we will be going through. We don't know how or whether the waivers will be granted," he said, explaining the terms banks might request were not yet known.
The Bank of New York backed the $15 million bond issue with a letter of credit, and the bonds are remarketed through the bank.

Maine Public Service officials noted that in the past the utility has won approval for such waivers. In a 10-K report that was filed in 1995, the company noted interest coverage tests were waived for a revolving credit line and a letter of credit that backed public utility bonds. The waivers were requested because of write-offs.

Maine Yankee has had safety-related shutdowns and is under close scrutiny by federal regulators. The plant and Entergy Corp recently signed an interim contract to run Maine Yankee while a longer-term management contract is negotiated.

The shutdown has hit Maine Public Service particularly hard as it draws around 35 percent of the power with which it supplies its customers from the plant, even though the utility only owns about a five percent stake in the plant.
Maine Public Service has said it had just over $41 million of long-term debt outstanding at year-end.
